questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.answer:
Yeah, sure. So I'm an AI/ML engineer with around five years of professional experience, mainly in Python, machine learning, and NLP, and more recently in generative AI, RAG, and AI agents.

I started my career at Accenture as an ML intern and later became a full-time engineer. There I worked on an enterprise knowledge platform, building NLP models with BERT for things like classification and entity extraction, and semantic search so people could find documents and past support tickets by meaning, not just keywords.

After moving to the U.S., I joined HCLTech, where I worked on an AI-powered developer assistant. It helped engineers search and understand code across a lot of repositories. I worked on the RAG side, so chunking, embeddings, vector search, and reranking, plus the backend APIs in FastAPI, all deployed on Azure.

Currently, I'm working with Perplexity through a contract vendor, focusing on multi-agent research, retrieval, and LLM evaluation. So I build agent workflows with LangChain and LangGraph that break complex questions into smaller parts, improve retrieval with hybrid search and reranking, and test every change with tools like RAGAS and A/B testing to make sure answers are grounded and accurate.

My contract ends in the next two weeks, so I'm looking for a long-term role where I can keep building impactful AI products, and really own systems from the data all the way to production.

questions.question: Can you walk me through your resume?
questions.answer: Absolutely. I started at Accenture in March 2020 as an ML intern, working on Python, SQL, and predictive modeling. My internship was extended, and I became a full-time ML Engineer in January 2021, working more with NLP and semantic search. After relocating to the U.S. and receiving work authorization, I joined HCLTech in June 2023 and worked on LLM-based developer tools and RAG. In January 2025, I moved to Perplexity on contract, focusing on multi-agent research and search quality. My career has evolved from traditional ML toward production generative AI.

questions.answer: I have around five years of professional AI/ML experience, starting with my Accenture internship in March 2020. I had a transition period when I relocated to the U.S., so I don't describe that as uninterrupted employment.

questions.answer: Pretty much my entire professional career has been focused on AI and machine learning. I started with predictive modeling and NLP, then moved toward deep learning, LLMs, RAG, and agentic AI.

questions.answer: Accenture gave me my foundation in Python, machine learning, and NLP. At HCLTech, I moved into enterprise generative AI and developer-assistant applications. Perplexity gave me the chance to work more deeply on multi-agent research, retrieval quality, and LLM evaluation. Each move was a natural step toward more advanced AI engineering.

questions.answer: My strongest language is Python, and my main focus is AI/ML engineering, especially LLMs, RAG, NLP, and AI agents. I've used LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, FAISS, Pinecone, FastAPI, SQL, PostgreSQL, Redis, AWS, Azure, Docker, and Kubernetes.

questions.answer: Python is definitely my strongest language. I've used it for data processing, ML and NLP pipelines, backend APIs, and LLM applications. I'm also comfortable working with SQL.

questions.answer: I'd say my strongest area is building end-to-end LLM applications, especially RAG pipelines, intelligent search, and agent workflows. I enjoy improving retrieval quality and turning models into reliable products.

questions.question: What kind of projects have you primarily worked on?
questions.answer: Most of my work has involved intelligent search, document understanding, developer assistants, and AI-powered research systems. Earlier in my career, I also worked on predictive models and NLP classification.

questions.answer: One of the most challenging projects was the multi-agent research system at Perplexity. We needed query understanding, retrieval, tool calling, and generation to work together while balancing answer quality and latency. I worked on retrieval tuning, reranking, and evaluation, which helped improve both relevance and performance.

questions.answer: I'm currently an AI/ML Engineer at Perplexity through a contract vendor. I work on LLM research workflows, RAG pipelines, intelligent search, and multi-agent systems, mainly improving retrieval and grounded response quality.

questions.question: Can you explain what you are currently working on at Perplexity?
questions.answer: I'm working on multi-agent research workflows. When someone asks a complex question, the system breaks it into smaller tasks, retrieves information from different sources, and combines the results. My work focuses on retrieval quality, reranking, agent orchestration, and evaluation.

questions.question: What does your typical day look like at Perplexity?
questions.answer: Usually, I start by checking current tasks and recent evaluation results. Then I spend time developing in Python, experimenting with retrieval strategies, improving agent workflows, or debugging issues. I also coordinate with engineers when changes affect other components. It's a mix of development, experimentation, and performance improvement.

questions.question: What are your main day-to-day responsibilities?
questions.answer: My day-to-day work includes building and improving RAG pipelines, integrating agent tools and APIs, evaluating LLM outputs, and optimizing retrieval and latency. I also work on Python backend services and troubleshooting system behavior.

questions.question: Can you explain your current project in simple, nontechnical terms?
questions.answer: Imagine asking an AI a question that needs information from several places. Instead of guessing, our system breaks the question into parts, searches for reliable information, and puts the findings together into one answer. I help make that process faster, more accurate, and more reliable.

questions.question: What was your specific contribution to the project?
questions.answer: My main contributions were in retrieval, evaluation, and agent workflow integration. I worked with hybrid search, reranking, and query understanding to improve which sources were found. Our project results included roughly 15% better Recall@10 and around 14% improvement in grounded-response quality.

questions.answer: I mainly use Python, LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, FAISS, Pinecone, FastAPI, and SQL. I've worked with LLMs including Sonar, GPT, Claude, and Llama, and evaluation tools such as RAGAS, LangSmith, and MLflow. On infrastructure, I've used AWS, Docker, Kubernetes, and Redis.

questions.answer: Both, actually. I independently own certain tasks, like experiments, features, or debugging, but I collaborate closely with the team on larger changes involving multiple services.

questions.answer: Yes, I've worked on production AI systems and deployment workflows, including inference and retrieval services, Docker containers, and AWS and Kubernetes-based environments. I've also worked on testing and monitoring deployed systems.

questions.question: What was the business impact of your work at Perplexity?
questions.answer: The main impact was improving response quality and speed. Our project results showed around 15% higher Recall@10, 14% better grounded-response quality, and about a 25% reduction in p95 research latency. That means more relevant answers with less waiting.

questions.question: How do you monitor models after deployment?
questions.answer: I look at both model quality and system health. For quality, I monitor retrieval relevance, groundedness, and evaluation scores. For system health, I check latency, errors, and resource usage. I've worked with MLflow, LangSmith, and CloudWatch to investigate changes and identify the source of problems.

questions.question: What was the biggest technical challenge you faced at Perplexity?
questions.answer: A major challenge was improving retrieval without making responses too slow. Multiple searches and reranking steps can add latency, so we experimented with retrieval strategies, caching, parallel execution, and model routing to balance quality and speed.

questions.question: Why are you leaving Perplexity?
questions.answer: My Perplexity role is contract-based, and it's coming to an end in the next two weeks. It's been a positive experience working on multi-agent systems and RAG, and I've received good feedback. I'm now looking for a long-term full-time opportunity with more end-to-end ownership.

questions.answer: The biggest lesson is that a good AI product needs much more than a powerful model. Retrieval, orchestration, evaluation, latency, and reliability all matter. I've learned how to balance those pieces in production systems.

questions.question: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
questions.answer: Supervised learning uses labeled examples, like predicting whether a transaction is fraudulent. Unsupervised learning uses unlabeled data to discover patterns, like grouping customers by behavior. The main difference is whether known target labels are provided during training.

questions.question: What is overfitting, and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: Overfitting happens when a model learns training examples and noise too closely, then performs poorly on new data. I address it with validation splits, cross-validation, regularization, early stopping, and controlling model complexity.

questions.question: Have you worked with deep learning frameworks such as PyTorch or TensorFlow?

questions.question: Have you worked with large language models?
questions.answer: Yes, I've worked extensively with LLMs including GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, and Sonar. My experience includes LLM integration, RAG, tool calling, agent workflows, prompt optimization, and evaluation.

questions.question: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
questions.answer: RAG means retrieving relevant information from external sources and giving it to a language model as context before it answers. It helps with current or private knowledge and makes answers more grounded in the source material.

questions.question: Have you built RAG-based applications?
questions.answer: Yes. RAG has been a major part of my work at HCLTech and Perplexity. I've worked on ingestion, chunking, embeddings, vector and hybrid search, reranking, generation, and retrieval evaluation.

questions.question: What is the difference between fine-tuning and RAG?
questions.answer: Fine-tuning updates model weights using training examples to change its behavior on a task. RAG leaves the model weights unchanged and supplies retrieved information at inference time. RAG is useful for changing knowledge; fine-tuning is useful for task-specific behavior.

questions.question: Have you worked with LangChain or LangGraph?
questions.answer: Yes, I've used both. LangChain helps connect models with retrievers, prompts, and tools. LangGraph helps build stateful, multi-step agent workflows with controlled execution. I've used them in developer-assistant and research systems.

questions.question: What are embeddings, and why are they useful?
questions.answer: Embeddings are numerical vectors representing the meaning of text or other data. Semantically similar phrases can have similar vectors even if they use different words. That's why embeddings are useful for semantic search and RAG.

questions.question: Which vector databases have you worked with?
questions.answer: I've worked with FAISS, Pinecone, and Azure AI Search for embedding-based retrieval. I'm also familiar with hybrid search combining vector similarity with keyword methods such as BM25.

questions.question: What is an AI agent?
questions.answer: An AI agent is a system that uses a model to decide what steps or tools to use to complete a task. For example, it might search, retrieve documents, analyze results, and produce an answer rather than just responding in one step.

questions.question: Have you worked with multi-agent systems?
questions.answer: Yes, multi-agent workflows are a key part of my Perplexity work. Complex tasks can be divided into research, retrieval, and analysis steps. I've worked with LangGraph, tool orchestration, and structured outputs to coordinate those components.

questions.question: How do you reduce hallucinations in LLM applications?
questions.answer: I start with reliable retrieval and source grounding, then use clear prompts, response validation, and evaluation. Tools like RAGAS and DeepEval help identify unsupported claims and whether the issue is retrieval or generation.
